clue.text: The uniform of a pupil arsonist?

definitions.text: The uniform of a pupil arsonist?

parts.words: The uniform of a pupil arsonist?
parts.note: the jacket a schoolchild wears is also, read literally, what you would call a schoolboy who sets fires

explanation.surface: A question about what a young fire-raiser wears to class.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue first describes the jacket of a school uniform; then 'pupil arsonist' asks for a school pupil who 'blazes', so the same phrase names the fire-starting pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: The jacket worn as part of British school uniform is called by this name, and a 'blazer' can also be one who sets things ablaze.

clue.text: A tutored study group remains to be mustered

indicators.note: mustering gathers and lines up troops afresh, so the letters of the fodder word are drawn up in a new order

explanation.surface: A tutor's class gathers whoever is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: A small university class where a tutor leads discussion is this kind of meeting.

clue.text: Grasp where the cargo is

explanation.definitionFit: To grip something is to keep it in one's hands, and a ship's lower storage space for freight shares the word.

clue.text: Heaven! My soul leaps about Hero's last follower!

indicators.note: about means going round, so the rearranged letters surround the other piece
the words my soul jump about wildly, so their letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the last letter of 'hero' is O, and the letter following O in the alphabet is P

explanation.surface: An ecstatic cry as a soul leaps after a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hero's last follower' is not a disciple: Hero's last letter is O, and the next letter of the alphabet is P. 'Leaps' scrambles MY SOUL into OLYMUS, and 'about' wraps it round the P.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the gods lived on this mountain, so it stands for the heavenly home of the deities.

clue.text: End of the recess, or of the working session?

definitions.text: End of the recess, or of the working session?

parts.words: End of the recess, or of the working session?
parts.note: the phrase for a school term finishing, when pupils go off on holiday, also describes a meeting dissolving

explanation.surface: A question about when the holiday or the meeting finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a school is said to do this when term ends and holidays begin, which here is cast as the 'end of the recess' loosely; a meeting that disperses does the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-word phrase means a gathering ending and its members dispersing, as a term ends for school holidays.

clue.text: An objection to border

parts.note: 'but' is a word used to object, as in 'no buts'

explanation.surface: Someone raises an objection about a boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: Land that touches a neighbouring plot along its edge is said to adjoin it.

clue.text: Farthest in line?

parts.note: the clue asks for the word for whatever sits at the very end of a row or queue

explanation.surface: A question about who is furthest along a queue.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means nearest the end, so in a row it is the item at the extreme position.

clue.text: The endearments that might reward a sugar-free slimming course

parts.words: that might reward a sugar-free slimming course
parts.note: a diet with no sugar in it would earn 'sweet' items amounting to nothing

explanation.surface: Lovers' talk as a prize for a dieter who has cut out sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: Endearments whispered by lovers carry this name; read literally, a sugar-free diet gives you no sweets at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Affectionate murmured words of little substance between lovers go by this idiom.

clue.text: A little perk from a bang?

definitions.text: A little perk from a bang?

parts.words: A little perk from a bang?
parts.note: a 'bang' is a hairstyle with hair cut straight across the forehead, so an advantage coming from it would come from that cut of hair

explanation.surface: A question about a small bonus resulting from an explosion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bang' looks like an explosion, but it is the American word for a straight-cut fringe of hair; a perk on top of salary is called by this phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra advantage an employer provides besides pay, such as a company car, is known by this phrase.

clue.text: F.A. eleven's final goal?

parts.note: the destination every football team in the Football Association Cup aims for is the stadium where the final is played

explanation.surface: A question about the last goal a football side scores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final goal' suggests the last score of a match; it means the target of reaching the Cup Final. This London stadium hosts the English FA Cup Final.
explanation.definitionFit: The national football stadium in London is where the Football Association's cup final is played, so every side aims to get there.

clue.text: A rude little company re-established in South America

indicators.note: something set up again in a new form, so the letters are rebuilt in a different order

parts.note: CO is the short form of company

explanation.surface: A small rude firm restarts its business on another continent.
explanation.definitionFit: The country lies on the Pacific coast of the continent, straddling the equator.

clue.text: Letters of no real sterling worth

definitions.text: Letters of no real sterling worth

parts.words: Letters of no real sterling worth
parts.note: the initials stamped on plated tableware show it is coated metal rather than true sterling silver

explanation.surface: A remark about documents that are worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sterling' looks like money; here it is sterling silver. The initials stand for electroplated nickel silver, a cheap imitation.
explanation.definitionFit: These initials mark electroplated nickel silver, a base metal coated to look like real silver.

clue.text: A revolutionary bar for road users

definitions.text: A revolutionary bar for road users

parts.words: A revolutionary bar for road users
parts.note: a rod that goes round and round as part of a wheel, on the bicycles and carts that use the road

explanation.surface: A rebel pub frequented by motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary bar' suggests a rebels' pub; it is a rod in a turning wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the rods joining the hub of a wheel to its rim goes by this name.

clue.text: Advance for a radio comedian

explanation.walkthrough: The Goon Show was a famous 1950s BBC radio comedy, whose performers were called Goons.
explanation.definitionFit: To proceed is to continue forward, and a member of the cast of the BBC's Goon Show was one of its clowns.

clue.text: Contagious terror of a grass

explanation.definitionFit: Sudden fear that spreads through a crowd has this name, and it is also the name of a genus of millet-like grasses.

clue.text: Near to being dexterous

explanation.definitionFit: Something close at hand is convenient, and a person skilled with their hands is adroit.

clue.text: Bellini's heroine, meeting Poles, made early conquests

definitions.note: the definition describes a people by what they did, standing for a plural noun

parts.note: Norma is the title heroine of Bellini's opera
N for north, one of the magnetic poles
S for south, the other pole

explanation.surface: An opera heroine meets Polish men and wins early romantic successes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people; it gives the two poles, N and S. The definition names the people by their deeds: the Normans conquered England in 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-Viking people from Normandy won England in 1066 and Sicily earlier still.

clue.text: For this Spanish dollar you might g-t star cooking in pastry

indicators.note: in places the cooked letters inside the pastry

parts.note: a pie is a dish made of pastry

indicators.note: cooking stirs the letters of star into something new

explanation.surface: A coin you might earn by cooking a star turn in a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' rearranges STAR as ASTR, and 'in' puts it inside PIE. The 'g-t' is the newspaper's rendering of 'get', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Spanish peso, the 'piece of eight', was known in English by this coin's name.

clue.text: Icing? That's super!

explanation.definitionFit: Icing is a covering on a cake, and as old British slang the word is an exclamation meaning excellent.

clue.text: Parodic burlesque of a a lancer in the ring

indicators.note: a burlesque mocks by distortion, so the fodder word is twisted into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A mocking send-up of a spearman in a bullring.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed has 'a a', a typesetting slip; one 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In bullfighting the horseman who goads the bull with a lance is this figure.

clue.text: The state of America Stalin was familiar with

explanation.definitionFit: One of the US states shares its name with Stalin's homeland in the Caucasus, where he was born.

clue.text: In modest fashion I become a dressmaker

indicators.note: to fashion something is to shape it, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Becoming a dressmaker while keeping a modest style.
explanation.definitionFit: A milliner or maker of fashionable women's clothes is known by this French-derived word.

clue.text: Staged on horseback?

explanation.definitionFit: A play put on is produced, and a rider seated on a horse is in the saddle.

clue.text: Girl tells stories in outbursts

parts.note: Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally or Sarah
to tell stories is a polite way of saying someone lies

explanation.surface: A girl spins tales in fits of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden witty remarks or sorties from a besieged force are both called by this word.

clue.text: Make a little progress in Winchester?

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit within the town's name

explanation.surface: A question about getting ahead in an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: To move forward slowly, a small distance at a time, is to edge along.

clue.text: Something extra from the boatswain, in short

indicators.note: the letters come from the short form, made over into a new order

parts.note: bosun is the shortened spelling of boatswain, a ship's officer

explanation.surface: A ship's officer hands out an extra.
explanation.walkthrough: The short form of 'boatswain' is BOSUN, whose letters are reordered; 'from' is the only signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An additional payment or benefit beyond what is due is a perk on top.

clue.text: A real sticker, so don't sniff!

definitions.text: A real sticker, so don't sniff!

parts.words: A real sticker, so don't sniff!
parts.note: the substance that makes things stick together is notoriously sniffed by solvent abusers

explanation.surface: A warning about a tenacious adhesive substance.
explanation.definitionFit: An adhesive paste or gum holds things together, and solvent abuse of it is a known danger.

clue.text: Link forged where wholesale firing takes place

indicators.note: forging hammers metal into a new shape, so the letters take a new form

explanation.surface: A chain link being hammered out where mass sackings happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firing' suggests dismissals; it is baking pottery or bricks in quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: An oven for baking pottery, bricks or lime fires its contents in bulk.

clue.text: When one is not bound to include royalty in the payment

indicators.note: to include means the payment takes in the royalty letter

parts.note: a fee is a payment for a service
R for Rex or Regina, king or queen

explanation.surface: A royalty is included in the charge so nobody is obliged.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrestrained or at liberty, someone without ties or obligations is at large.

clue.text: Did badly among rough set rushing here and there

indicators.note: among places the scrambled letters within the group

parts.note: a gang is a rough group of people

indicators.note: badly says the letters of did are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone performed poorly in a crowd of hooligans running about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges DID as DDI, which 'among' puts inside GANG.
explanation.definitionFit: Going about restlessly in pursuit of pleasure is gallivanting.

clue.text: Dead ends for linesmen?

parts.note: railway lines stop at end stations, so railwaymen would meet the places where the tracks finish

explanation.surface: A question about where football officials reach a dead end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesmen' suggests football officials; here they are railway workers, whose lines end at the final stations.
explanation.definitionFit: Stations at the ends of railway lines are the places where the track stops.

clue.text: Not the right speech delivered to a mistaken House

explanation.definitionFit: An inappropriate oration is an incorrect talk, and a letter sent to the wrong home went astray.
